item.title: China's yuan loans increase by 11.52 trln yuan in Jan.-Sept. period
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
China's yuan loans increase by 11.52 trln yuan in Jan.-Sept. period BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's yuan-denominated loans rose by 11.52 trillion yuan (about 1.71 trillion U.S. dollars) in the first three quarters of 2026, central bank data showed Wednesday. At the end of September, outstanding yuan loans stood at 283.44 trillion yuan, up 4.8 percent year on year, according to the People's Bank of China (PBOC). M2, a broad measure of money supply that covers cash in circulation and all deposits, stood at 359.63 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.2 percent year on year. M1, which covers currency in circulation, corporate demand deposits, personal demand deposits and provisions received by non-bank payment institutions, reached 116.76 trillion yuan at the end of September, a rise of 3.2 percent from a year earlier. China's outstanding aggregate financing to the real economy stood at 468.17 trillion yuan at the end of September, up 7.1 percent year on year, according to the central bank. "China's major financial aggregates have maintained reasonable growth, with M2 and aggregate financing to the real economy growing at appropriate rates," said Tian Xuan, dean of Peking University's Guanghua School of Management. "This has helped create a favorable monetary and financial environment for sustained economic improvement." Since the beginning of the year, the PBOC has introduced two rounds of structural monetary policy measures to address the needs of China's transition to new growth drivers and help financial institutions better align their services with the needs of the real economy. The latest round of structural monetary policy measures, announced in September, included cutting the one-year interest rate of the Pledged Supplementary Lending (PSL) facility from 1.75 percent to 1.5 percent, expanding the scope of PSL support, and increasing the quota of the relending facility for sci-tech innovation and technological upgrades by 200 billion yuan. The policy package will channel more funds to areas such as equipment upgrades, strengthen support for sci-tech enterprises, help ease financing constraints on private businesses and reduce their financing costs, said Dong Qingma, deputy head of the Institute of Chinese Financial Studies of Southwestern University of Finance and Economics. The effects of the September policy package are expected to emerge gradually, with existing and new monetary policy measures working in tandem to provide continued support for high-quality development of the real economy, experts said. item.title: Chinese mainland blasts Taiwan authorities' separatist rhetoric regarding history
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Chinese mainland blasts Taiwan authorities' separatist rhetoric regarding history BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- A Chinese mainland spokesperson on Wednesday criticized the Democratic Progressive Party (DPP) authorities in Taiwan, saying they had unscrupulously distorted history and hyped separatist rhetoric based on a warped version of history. Such rhetoric on history revealed the DPP authorities' true intention of inciting cross-Strait confrontation, said Chen Binhua, spokesperson for the State Council Taiwan Affairs Office, when responding to a media question on Taiwan authorities' and Lai Ching-te's remarks regarding the history of World War II. It also showed the DPP authorities' ignorance of history and betrayal of the ancestors, Chen said. The Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression was the first to break out and lasted the longest in the World Anti-Fascist War, or World War II, resulting in over 35 million Chinese military and civilian casualties from 1931 to 1945. The victory of the war and the recovery of Taiwan from Japanese occupation are great victories achieved by the Chinese people, including those in Taiwan, at the cost of blood and lives, Chen noted. Taiwan's liberation from the shackles of Japan's colonial rule and its return to the motherland represent an important outcome of the Chinese people's victory in fighting Japanese aggressors, and form an integral part of the post-World War II international order, Chen said. It's a historical memory the Chinese people across the Taiwan Strait should never forget, said Chen, urging compatriots in Taiwan to see the true face of the DPP authorities and stand on the right side of history. Following the Chinese people's victory in the war of resistance against Japanese aggressors, a full-blown civil war broke out between the forces led by the Communist Party of China (CPC) and the Chinese Kuomintang (KMT). In 1949, the remnants of the defeated KMT retreated to Taiwan, and the People's Republic of China was founded under the leadership of the CPC. This unresolved civil war and foreign interference have left the two sides of the Strait in a prolonged state of political confrontation, but the fact that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China's territory has never changed. The real status quo across the Taiwan Strait is that there is only one China in the world and that Taiwan is a part of China, Chen said. By promoting a false narrative of "democracy versus authoritarianism," stoking cross-Strait confrontation, or attempting to pursue "Taiwan independence" through military means and by relying on foreign forces, the DPP authorities will only gradually drag Taiwan into a dangerous situation and bring great disaster to the people in Taiwan, Chen noted. item.title: China's finance ministry outlines key agenda items for APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
China's finance ministry outlines key agenda items for APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- China's Ministry of Finance has introduced the key agenda items and expected outcomes of the APEC Finance Ministers' Meeting scheduled on Oct. 20 and 21 in Hong Kong. A ministry official said China will put forward four major topics -- fiscal policies to support people's livelihoods, financing of digital infrastructure, promoting inclusive finance tailored to local conditions, and fostering exchanges and cooperation among young finance professionals across APEC. Economies urgently need to strengthen macroeconomic policy coordination and adopt appropriate fiscal and financial policies to better support innovation and inclusive development, the official said. At the same time, the rapid advancement of digital technologies and artificial intelligence has generated new demand for digital infrastructure investment and financing, and highlighted the importance of improving exchanges among young finance professionals and strengthening future policy-making capacity, the official said. Finance ministers or their representatives from 21 APEC economies, along with senior representatives from relevant international organizations and partner institutions, will attend the meeting. At the meeting, representatives of APEC economies will hold in-depth exchanges and work toward consensus documents and deliverables on major topics, the official said. "Through these outcomes, we hope to pool useful experience from all parties, promote policy exchanges and experience sharing, and provide support for deepening Asia-Pacific financial cooperation and sustaining Asia-Pacific economic growth," the official said. The official said the meeting in Hong Kong will build up financial sector outcomes ahead of the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting, scheduled in Shenzhen in November. China stands ready to work with all APEC economies to uphold multilateralism, deepen macroeconomic policy coordination, maintain the stability and smooth functioning of regional industrial and supply chains, and jointly promote long-term sustainable economic growth in the Asia-Pacific to advance the building of the Asia-Pacific community, the official added. item.title: New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic An opening ceremony is held for a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on Oct. 15, 2026. (Xinhua/Pan Yulong) SHENYANG, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on Thursday, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery. The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between the city of Dandong in northeast China's Liaoning Province and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan Province in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The double-pylon and double-cable-plane bridge features a 28.5-meter-wide deck designed with four lanes for two-way traffic, while its water navigation clearance is designed for vessels of up to the 3,000-tonne class. The new bridge will further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Mao Ning said on Wednesday. China and the DPRK are friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, and the new bridge is an important facility for connectivity between the two countries, Mao noted at a regular press briefing. Dandong boasts China's largest border trade port with the DPRK. Before the new road bridge, the Yalu River Bridge, also known as the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge, served as a combined road-rail bridge. The old one, however, could only accommodate trucks weighing no more than 20 tonnes for one-way road traffic. China and the DPRK in 2010 agreed to build a new road bridge downstream from the old one. An opening ceremony is held for a new bridge across the Yalu River, the border river of China and the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK), on Oct. 15, 2026. item.title: China and the EU should be stable, balanced key trading partners
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
China and the EU should be stable, balanced key trading partners The second meeting of the China-EU trade and investment consultation mechanism was held in Beijing on Oct. 8 and 9. Guided by their commitment to maintaining stable and balanced trade ties as key trading partners, the two sides reviewed progress in various areas since the mechanism's first meeting, engaged in pragmatic and productive discussions, and agreed on a list of outcomes. They also issued a joint statement. At a time when the global economic recovery faces mounting pressure and anti-globalization sentiment is gaining ground, China and the EU have demonstrated how differences can be managed and cooperation advanced through equal, professional, and constructive dialogue within the framework of World Trade Organization (WTO) rules. Their efforts have provided a valuable source of stability for an uncertain world economy. The list of outcomes outlines 16 specific points of consensus covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights, and World Trade Organization (WTO) reform. These outcomes address shared concerns among industries on both sides and lay the groundwork for further cooperation. Delegates emphasized that the meeting marks a new beginning rather than a conclusion. This statement affirms that, despite their differences, China and the EU have the wisdom and capacity to find appropriate solutions, provided they uphold mutual respect, equality, and mutual benefit while acknowledging each other's legitimate concerns. International observers have widely welcomed the proceedings as a functional test of the consultation mechanism. By clarifying regulatory expectations and reducing uncertainty, the dialogue has helped stabilize market sentiment, delivering tangible benefits for Chinese and European enterprises alike, as well as for global economic stability. The essence of China-EU economic and trade relations lies in mutual benefit and win-win cooperation. The current structure of bilateral trade reflects the choices both sides have made based on their respective comparative advantages, and is a natural outcome of market forces. In 2025, trade in goods between China and the EU reached $828.11 billion, up 5.4 percent year on year, while their stock of two-way investment exceeded $280 billion. The two sides remained each other's second-largest trading partners. Despite rising protectionist headwinds, bilateral trade in goods grew 14.2 percent year on year to $447.88 billion in the first half of 2026. From automobiles and new energy to biomedicine and machinery, industries on both sides are deeply interconnected through supply chains and complement each other's strengths. Their markets are highly interdependent, and their shared interests are firmly established. Reaffirming their role as key trading partners, stabilizing bilateral economic and trade ties, and promoting more balanced trade are practical steps that reflect the depth of their economic integration, and demonstrate a shared sense of responsibility to provide greater certainty for the world. Europe has a profound tradition of free trade and has long been an important builder of an open world economy. China has noted that, in recent years, the EU has introduced a series of trade remedy measures and industrial policies whose spillover effects have attracted international attention. Politicizing economic and trade issues, expanding the concept of national security to cover an ever-wider range of issues, and erecting unreasonable barriers to trade and investment run counter to the WTO principle of fair competition. Such measures can also disrupt the stability of global industrial and supply chains and ultimately undermine the upgrading and transformation of European industries themselves. An analysis by The Economist gets to the heart of the matter: if Europe wants a thriving industrial sector, its focus should not be on keeping competitors out, but on addressing its own internal problems. Similar views echo among European business leaders, who argue that enhancing competitiveness requires addressing internal structural bottlenecks instead of limiting foreign competition. China maintains that it has consistently partnered with Europe to overcome development challenges, rather than creating them. The principal risk to bilateral economic relations today lies not in natural trade flows, but in using "de-risking" as a justification for strategic disengagement. China has consistently maintained that interdependence is not a risk, interconnected interests are not a threat, and openness and cooperation are the right path to shared development. China's vast market, rapidly evolving innovative applications and complete industrial support system are indispensable to Europe's green transition and efforts to spur scientific and technological innovation. According to the German Chamber of Commerce in China, decades of operational experience in the Chinese market have equipped German firms with competitive advantages that strengthen their global footprint. As unilateralism and protectionist policies gain traction worldwide, the integrity of the international trading system faces mounting stress. Both China and the EU reaffirm their support for a rules-based multilateral order, endorse WTO modernization, and stress strict adherence to agreed disciplines. Aligning on these principles is vital not only for bilateral prosperity but for global economic governance at large. Sustained dialogue and mutually beneficial cooperation remain the most effective tools for managing differences and expanding common ground. Looking ahead, China stands prepared to work closely with the EU to address trade concerns through continuous consultation, grounded in WTO compliance and mutual respect for core interests. By deepening engagement, both sides can unlock new commercial opportunities, reinforce global supply chain resilience, and contribute to a more open, inclusive, and stable world economy. (Zhong Sheng is a pen name often used by People's Daily to express its views on foreign policy and international affairs.) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Indigo dyeing of Dong ethnic group brings prosperity in SW China's Guizhou
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Indigo dyeing of Dong ethnic group brings prosperity in SW China's Guizhou Vats of indigo dye ripple gently in the workshop as visitors stream through the sales area at the traditional crafts farmers' cooperative in Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. Photo shows the traditional crafts farmers' cooperative in Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) "Here, traditional ethnic culture is reflected in distinctive products designed for everyday use," said Lu Yongmei, head of the cooperative and a provincial-level representative inheritor of Dong indigo dyeing. Indigo dyeing is deeply rooted in the daily lives of the Dong people in Zhaoxing Dong Village, one of the largest Dong villages in the country. It is both a traditional craft and an important means of passing down their culture. Lu Yongmei arranges creative cultural products at the traditional crafts farmers' cooperative in Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (People's Daily Online/Tu Min) In 2014, Lu, who learned to spin yarn and grow indigo plants with her mother from an early age and grew up in her grandfather's dyeing workshop, took the lead in establishing the cooperative. She visited artisans in more than 100 nearby villages to rescue and revive endangered techniques. The cooperative also began collecting and restoring old embroidered pieces. Initially, the cooperative focused on traditional Dong ceremonial attire. However, limited occasions for wearing it and a lack of broader appeal led to unsold stock. In 2016, the cooperative ran into a cash-flow crisis. Lu soon shifted its focus, repurposing traditional Dong fabrics, drawing on classic ethnic motifs and adapting traditional techniques to modern tastes to create creative cultural products for everyday use. Photo shows an aerial view of Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) "Traditional crafts once emphasized full, elaborate designs and striking visual effects to showcase craftsmanship. For our new products, we use lighter colors and techniques such as tie-dyeing, preserving the fabric's texture while reducing production time and complexity," Lu said. However, the approach met with strong opposition from some villagers and veteran embroiderers. Nevertheless, Lu pressed ahead with her vision. She changed the product forms while preserving traditional techniques, embracing innovation without losing sight of the craft's roots. The cooperative kept traditional production processes while adapting product designs and the use of motifs. Sales of its first batch of creative cultural products exceeded 100,000 yuan (about $14,939), causing those initially opposed to come around. Visitors try their hand at traditional crafts at the traditional crafts farmers' cooperative in Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Alongside product innovation, Lu led her team in cataloging more than 300 traditional Dong motifs and building a digital pattern library. The cooperative also introduced hands-on workshops, giving visitors the chance to experience the craft firsthand. "In 2025, the cooperative's annual output value exceeded 20 million yuan, providing more than 1,000 Dong women with jobs and opportunities to earn income close to home," said Lu. Photo shows indigo-dyed products on display in the store at the traditional crafts farmers' cooperative in Zhaoxing Dong Village, Liping county, Qiandongnan Miao and Dong Autonomous Prefecture, southwest China's Guizhou Province. (People's Daily Online/Yang Qian) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: "China Hotline" helps foreigners plug into people-centered governance
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
"China Hotline" helps foreigners plug into people-centered governance This undated photo shows the 24-hour Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center in Beijing, capital of China. (Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center/Handout via Xinhua) BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- After "China Travel" draws global travelers to its capital, China is offering the world another way in: the "China Hotline," a 12345 service that lets foreign nationals make their voices heard and help improve the city they reside in. The service is part of a broader reform that began in Beijing in 2019, when the city, home to over 20 million residents, launched a "swift response to public complaints" initiative. The goal is to address concerns promptly and resolve everyday challenges efficiently. More than 60 hotline services have been integrated into a single number, 12345, which now serves as the main channel for residents to report issues. Operating 24/7, the hotline is staffed by over 1,700 operators who work in shifts to take calls and handle requests covering nearly every aspect of urban life, including transportation, housing, education, healthcare, employment and business services. Foreign visitors and residents in Beijing are covered by the service, where they are treated not as outsiders but as part of the city. Official data shows the Chinese capital has handled about 200 million public appeals in just over seven years, with resolution and satisfaction rates both exceeding 97 percent. "The experience of Beijing's citizen service system offered valuable lessons for Athens in advancing people-centered urban governance and building a city that listens to its citizens and responds to their concerns," said Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece, during the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints. The two-day event, which opened Monday, brought together more than 3,200 participants from over 70 countries and regions to explore new paths for modernizing urban governance, a challenge shared across the world. Georgios K. Giannaros, first deputy mayor of Athens, Greece, addresses the opening ceremony of the 2026 Beijing Forum on Swift Response to Public Complaints in Beijing, capital of China, Oct. 12, 2026. (Xinhua/Xie Han) OPEN HOTLINE Marie, an expat living in Beijing, once hit a snag when signing up for a water show on the Grand Canal in Tongzhou District: the online registration form on WeChat only accepted Chinese mainland resident ID cards, leaving no way to enter foreign passport details. After Marie raised the issue through the 12345 hotline, the case was assigned to Tongzhou authorities, who activated a fast-track mechanism for requests involving foreign nationals. Working with the platform operator and its technical team, they upgraded the registration system within just one working day, adding a field for passports and other foreign ID documents. The 12345 hotline's foreign-related services are not only efficient, but also expanding in both scope and capacity. "Foreign callers have all kinds of requests, with visa and entry-exit policies and work permit applications among the most common inquiries," said Wang Dongbo, an English-language operator on the hotline, adding that whether they live in Beijing or are just visiting briefly, foreigners who run into trouble can call 12345, and someone will see the matter through. "Besides our dedicated English lines, calls in other languages are transferred to the multilingual service center at Beijing Foreign Studies University, where volunteers join in on a three-way call," said Shan Qiang with the Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center. The hotline now provides round-the-clock services in eight foreign languages. Beyond the hotline, Beijing has rolled out "12345 Online," a digital platform offering the same service. Meanwhile, a multi-dimensional support network for foreigners is taking shape in the Chinese capital. The network spans "GO BEIJING" -- a one-stop service platform for overseas visitors -- the English edition of Beijing's official public services app, the International Web Portal of Beijing and airport service points, responding to their needs at every stage, from pre-trip planning and entry, to life in Beijing. "In the governance logic of China's capital, where every complaint gets a response, the 'people' in 'the people's voices are heard' now include foreigners living in Beijing," said Zhang Yi, director of the institute for capital governance at the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences. SHARED GOVERNANCE Being heard is only part of the story. Traik Souhail from Morocco spends almost every weekend studying at Beijing Library in Tongzhou District. He noticed that seat-hogging was a common problem here. "Public resources shouldn't sit idle or go to waste. Every seat should go to someone who actually needs it," he said. In August last year, he submitted a proposal through "12345 Online," suggesting the library set a 30-minute limit on unoccupied seats to stop long-term seat-hogging. After verifying the situation, the library moved quickly to address this issue. It posted notices in Chinese and English urging readers to use the library respectfully and refrain from hogging seats, stepped up manual patrols, and promptly cleared unattended items from seats, bringing order back to its reading areas. Li Wenzhao, a professor at the School of Public Administration and Policy, Renmin University of China, said Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" has transformed the traditional top-down model of urban governance into a collaborative, multi-stakeholder approach. It is equally open to foreign residents, encouraging them to take ownership and bring international perspectives, experience and expertise into the capital's governance. "Cities become more beautiful through openness, which is also essential to a world-class, harmonious and livable capital," he said. "Anyone who lives in this city has a channel to voice concerns and take part in governance. The hotline not only bridges language barriers but also opens a path for diverse groups to integrate into urban governance," said Yao Lei, director of the Beijing Citizen Hotline Service Center. CHINESE SOLUTION In June, more than 20 young scholars from leading think tanks across Latin America visited the 12345 hotline call center in Beijing. "Over 20 million appeals a year. That's incredible!" Chilean scholar Maria Fernanda Garredon said after seeing the full call-handling process for herself. "If residents didn't find it effective, they wouldn't call. Such a high volume shows that once you get through, your concerns are heard and solutions are found." In recent years, the center has hosted nearly 2,500 foreign visitors from more than 120 countries, including the United States, Belarus and Thailand. Belarusian delegations have visited three times to learn from the hotline's experience, and the country plans to draw on Beijing's 12345 model to set up its own hotline. "When you set foot on Chinese soil, see firsthand how institutions operate and learn how ordinary people get their problems solved, you come to understand that China is truly committed to improving people's livelihoods and tackling real problems," said Salvadoran scholar Juan Gilberto Contreras Gomez. "There is a global phenomenon unfolding in Western countries, developing countries and elsewhere. People don't feel that governments respond to their needs or their immediate problems -- mainly services and quality of life," said Omar Razzaz, a senior fellow at Harvard Kennedy School and former prime minister of Jordan. He has been actively promoting Beijing's "swift response to public complaints" reform at various international events. Razzaz called the 12345 citizen hotline "a model of efficient and balanced governance," noting that it represents a deep integration of technological empowerment and institutional innovation. "I've seen elements of it in different countries. But the way it worked here was quite impressive, and I felt like China should share that experience," he added. item.title: China's energy push set to fuel long-term global energy resilience
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
China's energy push set to fuel long-term global energy resilience An aerial drone photo shows auxiliary lines of the Hami-Chongqing ±800 kV ultra-high voltage direct current transmission project, in Hami, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, March 21, 2025. (Xinhua/Ding Lei) BEIJING, Oct. 14 (Xinhua) -- As the world confronts what the International Energy Agency (IEA) has described as the most severe energy crisis in its history, China, the world's largest crude importer, has chosen restraint over panic, helping stabilize global oil markets. Rather than scrambling to secure supplies after the Strait of Hormuz, one of the planet's most critical oil choke points, was thrown into turmoil in late February, China has reduced its crude purchases, released strategic reserves to meet domestic needs, and drawn on its increasingly diversified supply channels and expanding renewable energy capacity. The result, according to IEA Executive Director Fatih Birol, has been a meaningful cushion for a market reeling from the largest supply disruption in modern history. On the demand side, China has played an important role in stabilizing markets by reducing its crude oil imports by nearly 50 percent compared with pre-war levels, Birol said in a statement, while noting that significant supplies from Gulf producers and increased exports from the United States, Brazil, Venezuela and Kazakhstan have also helped offset some of the losses from the Gulf. China's restraint has not been accidental. It reflects a viable, multi-layered energy strategy that has been quietly reshaping the country's role in the global energy order: from a passive price-taker vulnerable to geopolitical tremors to an anchor of stability with domestic policy choices now rippling outward, resulting in tangible, positive outcomes for the world economy. A drone photo taken on March 23, 2025 shows a 50-megawatt molten-salt solar thermal power plant in Naomaohu Township of Hami City, northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Ding Lei) OIL PURCHASE RESTRAINT Customs data tell a striking story. In the first nine months of 2026, China's crude oil imports totaled 358 million tonnes, a year-on-year decline of 15.3 percent. This contraction deepened sharply in June, when imports fell to 29.27 million tonnes -- down 41.3 percent from a year earlier and 11.5 percent from May, marking the lowest monthly figure since October 2016. Chen Shouhai, director of the oil and gas policy and law research center at China University of Petroleum in Beijing, anticipates a short-term rebound in imports as restocking demand kicks in during the early stages of any de-escalation, but he cautions that this would represent only a cyclical inventory correction, not a reversal of the underlying demand trend. Over a three-to-five-year horizon, China's total crude imports are likely to decline gradually, according to Chen. The logic is structural, with China's oil consumption having already passed its peak, seeing refined product demand falling year by year since 2024. Petrochemical feedstock demand continues to grow modestly, but nowhere near enough to offset the erosion in transport fuel consumption. Meanwhile, domestic exploration and production have strengthened steadily, with output rising and the import dependency ratio of roughly 70 percent expected to ease. China's commitment to and pursuit of peaking carbon dioxide emissions before 2030 and achieving carbon neutrality before 2060, coupled with rapid advances in wind, solar and new energy vehicle (NEV) technologies, is fundamentally compressing oil demand. China's decision not to hit the panic button has drawn international attention. Nicholas Wagner, manager of energy initiatives at the World Economic Forum, observed in an analysis of how the war in the Middle East is reshaping Asia's energy transition: "China appears to be somewhat shielded from Middle East conflict-driven price shocks by its significant energy reserves, diversified energy supply and rapidly expanding renewable energy sector, which together reduce its dependence on Middle Eastern oil. This lesson will not be lost on policymakers." A staff member inspects equipment in Jiqing Oilfield operation area of Xinjiang Oilfield Company of China National Petroleum Corporation (CNPC) in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, Aug. 30, 2026. (Xinhua/Ding Lei) STRATEGIC ENERGY PUSH Domestic scholars argue that China's composure amid this global energy tsunami is no accident. It is the product of a strategic architecture first articulated in 2014 -- promoting revolutions in energy consumption, supply, technology and institutions while strengthening international cooperation across the board. Data from the National Energy Administration revealed that in 2025, China's primary energy production had reached 5.13 billion tonnes of standard coal equivalent, with domestic crude oil output hitting 216 million tonnes and natural gas production exceeding 260 billion cubic meters, all record highs. China's energy self-sufficiency rate climbed to 84.4 percent in 2025 and is expected to rise further in 2026. Alongside this domestic expansion, China has constructed a "land-sea linkage, multi-corridor parallel" energy import architecture, with crude oil imported from 49 countries and natural gas from more than 20 countries. Xiao Hongwei, a research fellow at the National Development and Reform Commission, sees the first half of 2026 as a period of multiple breakthroughs in supply security and green transition. China's oil and gas production continued to set records in this period: industrial crude oil output reached 109.43 million tonnes, while natural gas production hit 133 billion cubic meters, both all-time highs for the period. Installed power generation capacity surpassed 4 billion kilowatts, up 10.8 percent year-on-year, maintaining the country's position as the world leader, with non-fossil energy accounting for 62 percent of installed capacity. For the first time, coal-fired power generation fell below 50 percent of total electricity output, while renewable sources exceeded 40 percent, a signal that wind and solar are playing greater roles in China's power mix. Energy efficiency has continued to improve as well. Preliminary calculations show energy consumption grew 2.7 percent in the first half of 2026, with the growth rate decelerating by 1.2 percentage points from the first quarter. Coal's share in the consumption mix held steady, oil's share declined by one percentage point, and clean energy's share rose by one percentage point, serving as evidence that green and low-carbon energy use is becoming an increasingly automatic choice across industries and households. The most visible transformation, however, is in transportation. According to the China Association of Automobile Manufacturers, NEV production and sales both exceeded 10.6 million units in the first eight months of 2026, with year-on-year growth of more than 10 percent, while NEVs accounted for 52.4 percent of all new vehicle sales. Zhao Qibo, an economist based in Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region in northwest China, said China's long-standing efforts to diversify its energy transport routes, sources and types have clearly paid off. As a stabilizing anchor for national energy security, Xinjiang has abundant oil and coal resources in the traditional energy sector, providing solid support for the country's energy supply. At the same time, Xinjiang's vast land has irreplaceable advantages in wind and solar resources, supplying strong support for sustainable energy development. An aerial drone photo taken on May 29, 2026 shows new energy vehicles waiting to be loaded onto a vessel at a logistics base in Nantong City, east China's Jiangsu Province. (Photo by Xu Congjun/Xinhua) POTENTIAL BOOST TO WORLD ENERGY FUTURE In June, China released its first-ever five-year plan for building a new energy system, targeting the initial establishment of a clean, low-carbon, safe and efficient energy architecture by 2030. This month, meanwhile, China issued a set of guidelines aimed at accelerating the development of new quality productive forces. The energy revolution has been elevated to an unprecedented level, and nuclear power, photovoltaics, energy storage and hydrogen energy have received clear policy endorsement. Hu Ming, Party secretary of China Electric Power Planning and Engineering Institute, describes the coming five years as a period of overlapping security risks and accelerating low-carbon transition. International instability will continue to test the resilience of energy systems, while China's own commitments, including a 17-percent reduction in carbon dioxide emissions per unit of GDP and a 10-percent decline in energy consumption per unit of GDP, will demand an intensification of the green transition. Under the plan, China will strengthen new energy infrastructure construction, pursue a diversified portfolio spanning wind, solar, hydropower and nuclear power, and expand non-fossil energy supply at scale. This includes steadily advancing coastal nuclear power, offshore wind and distributed new energy development, while actively promoting clean energy bases and transmission corridors in its northern regions and integrated hydro-solar-wind projects in the southwest. Michal Meidan, head of China energy research at the Oxford Institute for Energy Studies, argues that the U.S.-Iran conflict has demonstrated the efficacy of China's energy strategy. "China's dependence on imported oil remains substantial, but the geopolitics of energy are shifting from control of oil flows to control of electrified industrial systems," she wrote in a signed article, noting China's clear head start in this transition. Hu also sees the current period as a critical window for speeding up international cooperation in China's energy industry. The present circumstances, he argues, favor leveraging China's industrial strengths in energy technology to expand green industry collaboration and help shape a new pattern of global energy governance. From grid interconnections and clean energy supply chains to technology transfer and joint standards development, opportunities for partnership are expanding just as the global demand for energy resilience has never been more urgent. Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air, noted that China's exports of batteries, wind turbines, electric vehicles and, above all, solar panels helped avoid 374 million metric tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions globally in 2025, which is more carbon dioxide emissions than Britain produced last year. Calculated over the full lifecycle of these products, China's clean technology exports shipped in 2025 are projected to avoid a total of 6.9 billion tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions over their operating lifetimes. This is a 31-percent increase compared with the 2024 estimate and equivalent to roughly twice India's carbon emissions in 2025, according to the expert. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. Xi's article on advancing Party self-governance to be published (Xinhua) 15:45, October 15, 2026 BEIJING, Oct. 15 (Xinhua) -- An article by Xi Jinping, general secretary of the Communist Party of China (CPC) Central Committee, on advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance with higher standards and more concrete measures will be published on Friday. The article by Xi, also Chinese president and chairman of the Central Military Commission, will be published in this year's 20th issue of the Qiushi Journal, a flagship magazine of the CPC Central Committee.
